title: Pull a midget fuse from its open-clip block with a tong puller held across it, and put it in the parts tray
instruction: The panel is locked out and tested dead. Use the fuse puller to take out the middle fuse, F2, and put it in the parts tray.
context: Electricians (O*NET 47-2111.00; about 821,000 US jobs in 2025, BLS Occupational Outlook Handbook) "Repair or replace wiring, equipment, or fixtures, using hand tools or power tools" and "Diagnose malfunctioning systems ... using test equipment and hand tools". Pulling a control-circuit fuse to test or replace it is everyday panel work. Midget fuses sit 20 mm apart in spring clips, too close for fingers, so electricians use a nylon tong puller: held square to the fuse, its jaws close round the body between the clips, the fuse is drawn out of both clips, and it goes in a tray, not loose in the panel.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0. A gray steel wall-mount enclosure, 20 x 16 x 6 in (50.8 tall, 40.6 wide, 15.2 deep), stands bolted upright on the bench with its open front toward the robot at x 27.3 (back at x 42.5, sides at y -20.3 and 20.3) and its door off. Its white back pan faces the robot at x 40.8. A 35 mm top-hat DIN rail runs across it horizontally at height 15 (its top at x 40.05), with six gray terminal blocks on its left part. On the rail, centered at y 0, is a black Bussmann BMM603-3SQ three-pole midget fuse block (7.7 tall, 6.0 wide, 3.3 deep off the rail, front at x 36.75). It holds three Bussmann FNM 13/32 x 1-1/2 in fuses (10.3 mm x 38.1 mm, brown fiber tube, tinned ferrules 9.5 mm long, about 9 g) standing upright, their middles at height 15 and their axes at x 37.25: F1 at y 2, F2 at y 0, F3 at y -2 (9.7 mm apart tube to tube), marked F1 to F3 on the block's marker strip below each pole. Each ferrule sits in a tinned copper spring clip: the clip base behind it and two fingers up its sides to just past its widest point. Barriers stand between the poles beside the clips, and screw-terminal housings stand beyond each fuse end to the block's front; behind the middle of each fuse's tube the block is recessed 7 mm. A yellow Ideal 34-015 nylon tong fuse puller (sold as 5 in; modeled 12.2 from loop to jaw tips, about 20 g, jaws 17 mm open at rest) lies flat on the bench along x, loop end at x 15, y -10, jaw tips toward the panel at x 27.2, on a tape outline. A blue plastic parts tray, 15 x 10 x 3 cm, sits loose on the bench centered at x 20.5, y -26, on a tape outline. Positions are set with a tape measure from marks on the bench to within 2 mm; the enclosure is bolted down and the rail and block do not move between trials. Both arms start at their ready pose. One fixed layout.
scoring: Scored on F2's state at the end, after two checks kept over the whole trial. 0 for the trial if F1 or F3 is ever out of either clip for two control steps in a row: a ferrule's center more than 2.5 mm out of its seat (past the fingers' lips), or 3 mm off the clip sideways or 5 mm along the fuse; a real trial measures each after the run with a caliper's depth rod from the barrier front beside each ferrule (more than 2.6 mm proud means out; seated reads about 0.2 mm) and checks the video for when. At most 0.5 for the trial if F2 ever leaves its second clip without the puller's jaws closed round its body at that step or the one before (both jaws on the tube, each face at most 1 mm off it, on opposite sides of it, between the ferrules), even if it is put back and pulled properly later; a real trial checks the robot's wrist-camera frames where F2's second ferrule leaves its clip. Otherwise: 1.0 with F2 out of both clips, its middle inside the tray's walls (any position or way up; on the final overhead photo), released (a release check: neither jaw nor any gripper in contact with it, contact meaning its own shape within 2 mm) still (under 2 cm/s for the last second, from the final photo and video), and the puller put down: lying flat on the bench anywhere outside the enclosure and the tray, both arms on the bench, no gripper in contact with it (the job is not finished while the tool is still in hand; checked on the final photo); 0.75 with F2 in the tray but still held or moving, or the puller still in hand or not put down; 0.5 with F2 out of both clips anywhere else (held, or dropped on the bench); 0.25 with F2 dropped loose inside the enclosure, where it must be found before power goes back on; 0.25 with one end of F2 out of its clip, the fuse cocked in the block; 0 with F2 still in both clips, including doing nothing. How the fuse comes out (one end first or straight), where on the bench the puller is laid and where the arms end up are not scored. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0.
reset_notes: Push F2 back into its clips by hand until both ferrules seat on the clip bases; with a caliper's depth rod, check each of the three fuses' ferrule fronts stands no more than 0.5 mm proud of the barrier fronts beside it (seated, about 0.2 mm). Lay the puller flat back on its tape outline, loop end toward the robot, jaws toward the panel; empty the tray and set it back on its outline. Check the outlines to within 2 mm with a tape measure.
fidelity: Real sizes. Each clip is its fingers and base as colliders plus a law: it presses its ferrule onto the base with 6 N (assumed; not published) until the ferrule's center is 2.5 mm out, past the lips. The tong's flex is a spring hinge at the loop. The tube collides as a 9.6 mm square prism. Rigid contacts have no rolling resistance, so the fuse has angular damping (4/s) instead. Nothing attaches the fuse to the puller or the hand.
